Isaiah 57.summary: The righteous are taken away without their neighbors recognizing what it means (Isaiah 57:1–2). A sharp denunciation confronts idolatrous practices and unfaithfulness (Isaiah 57:3–13). The Lord then promises revival to the contrite but denies peace to the wicked (Isaiah 57:14–21).
Isaiah 57.whereWeAre: Chapter 56 denounced leaders too negligent to notice real danger. Here that same blindness shows itself again: the righteous are taken away and no one even registers what their loss means, while the chapter sharply denounces the community's idolatry before promising revival to the humble and contrite, though never peace to the wicked. Chapter 58 exposes a related blindness, a community that fasts sincerely while still oppressing the people around it.

keyFigures.name: the contrite
keyFigures.role: Those promised divine dwelling and healing.

keyThemes.explanation: The righteous perishing while 'no man layeth it to heart' names a community too distracted to notice its own real losses.
Describing idolatry as adultery, 'thou hast discovered thyself to another than me,' frames unfaithfulness to God in the same terms as betrayal of a marriage.
God's promise to dwell 'with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit' pairs his own high and lofty dwelling with deliberate nearness to the lowest and most broken.

Isaiah 58.summary: God exposes a community that fasts while exploiting laborers and quarreling (Isaiah 58:1–5). The fast God favors loosens oppression, feeds the hungry, shelters the homeless, and clothes the naked (Isaiah 58:6–12). Honoring the Sabbath brings delight in the Lord (Isaiah 58:13–14).
Isaiah 58.whereWeAre: Chapter 57 promised healing to the humble but no peace to the wicked. Here that same gap between appearance and reality becomes very specific: a community fasts sincerely while still exploiting its own laborers, and God insists that the fast he actually wants loosens oppression, feeds the hungry, and shelters the homeless instead. Chapter 59 widens this same concern for justice, insisting that it is violence and injustice, not any failure of God's power, that has separated the people from him.

keyThemes.explanation: A fast where people ask 'have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge?' while still striking others 'with the fist of wickedness' exposes a religious practice that coexists comfortably with ongoing cruelty.
The fast God chooses is defined almost entirely in physical, practical terms, undoing bonds, sharing bread, housing the homeless, rather than religious ritual alone.
Calling the Sabbath 'a delight' rather than a burden reframes a commanded rest as something to be genuinely enjoyed, not merely endured.

Isaiah 59.summary: The chapter insists God's power has not failed; violence, lies, and injustice have separated the people from him (Isaiah 59:1–8). A communal confession acknowledges darkness and failed justice (Isaiah 59:9–15). The Lord takes up the cause of righteousness and announces a redeemer for Zion and an enduring covenant Spirit (Isaiah 59:16–21).
Isaiah 59.whereWeAre: Chapter 58 named practical injustice as the real obstacle to God's blessing. Here that same point is pressed further: God's power has not grown too short to save, it is the people's own violence and lies that have separated them from him, until a communal confession of failed justice leads the Lord to take up the cause of righteousness himself, promising both a redeemer and an enduring covenant Spirit. Chapter 60 answers that promised redemption with a vision of Zion rising, finally, into glory.

keyFigures.name: The sinful community
keyFigures.role: People accused and later confessing guilt.

keyFigures.name: redeemer
keyFigures.role: Promised deliverer for those turning from transgression.

keyThemes.explanation: Insisting that God's 'hand is not shortened' redirects blame away from any limit on God's power and onto sins that have actively come between the people and him.
A shared confession that 'we roar all like bears' and grope for a wall like blind men admits collective failure honestly, without singling out one group to blame.
God 'saw that there was no man' to intervene and so acted himself, putting on righteousness and salvation like armor when no human effort proved sufficient.

explainedReferences.explanation: Words about feet swift to shed blood and not knowing peace.

Isaiah 60.summary: Zion is summoned to rise and shine because the Lord's glory has come (Isaiah 60:1–3). Nations and kings bring children, wealth, and rebuilding help to her gates (Isaiah 60:4–16). Violence ends and God becomes her everlasting light (Isaiah 60:17–22).
Isaiah 60.whereWeAre: Chapter 59 promised that God himself would intervene when no one else could. Here that intervention arrives as glory: Zion is summoned to rise and shine because the Lord's own glory has come, with nations and kings bringing children, wealth, and rebuilding help to her gates until violence ends and God himself becomes her everlasting light. Chapter 61 narrows this grand vision to a single anointed speaker, sent to announce that same good news directly to the poor.

keyThemes.explanation: Zion's light draws nations and kings 'to the brightness of thy rising,' picturing restoration as something so visible it attracts attention from far beyond Israel's own borders.
Children, wealth, and even cedar wood arriving from foreign nations combine Zion's people returning with the physical material needed to rebuild what was lost.
God replacing the sun and moon as Zion's 'everlasting light' pictures a peace secure enough that it no longer depends on anything as changeable as daylight.

Isaiah 61.summary: An anointed speaker announces good news to the poor, freedom to captives, and comfort to mourners (Isaiah 61:1–3). Ruins will be rebuilt and a priestly people will enjoy an enduring covenant (Isaiah 61:4–9); the chapter ends with a song of salvation and righteousness (Isaiah 61:10–11).
Isaiah 61.whereWeAre: Chapter 60 pictured Zion's rising glory drawing nations to her light. Here a single anointed speaker is sent to bring that same good news directly to individuals: liberty for captives, comfort for mourners, and rebuilt ruins for a people who will be called priests of the Lord. Chapter 62 continues in that speaker's own voice, refusing to stay silent until Zion's righteousness is finally visible to everyone.

keyFigures.name: Anointed speaker
keyFigures.role: Unnamed herald empowered by the Lord's Spirit.

keyThemes.explanation: Being anointed specifically 'to preach good tidings unto the meek' and bind up the brokenhearted directs this speaker's mission toward people usually overlooked.
Promising that 'they shall build the old wastes' turns long-ruined places into a future project, not a permanent loss.
Comparing righteousness to a garment and a bride's jewels pictures moral renewal as something worn with visible joy, not simply followed as a rule.

explainedReferences.explanation: From Isaiah's passage concerning the anointed one bringing good news and liberation; the wording is not identical.
This passage in the synagogue at Nazareth.
Proclamation of the acceptable year of the Lord; he does not quote the entire verse.

Isaiah 62.summary: The speaker refuses silence until Zion's righteousness shines and she receives a new name (Isaiah 62:1–5). Watchmen are appointed to keep calling on God (Isaiah 62:6–9), and the chapter summons preparations for returning people and heralds the city's redemption (Isaiah 62:10–12).
Isaiah 62.whereWeAre: Chapter 61 closed with a song celebrating salvation and righteousness. Here the speaker takes up that same hope as a personal commitment, refusing to stay silent until Zion's righteousness is visible and she receives a new name, while watchmen are appointed to keep calling on God and the way is prepared for her returning people. Chapter 63 turns from this patient, hopeful watching to a sudden, dramatic scene of judgment, a warrior arriving from Edom.

keyFigures.name: Zion (Jerusalem)
keyFigures.role: City portrayed as bride and newly named community.

keyThemes.explanation: The vow to 'not hold my peace' and to 'not rest' until Zion's vindication arrives models prayer as sustained, active persistence rather than a single request.
Being renamed Hephzibah, 'my delight is in her,' instead of Forsaken replaces an old identity defined by rejection with one defined by being wanted.
Watchmen set on the walls specifically to 'give him no rest' until Jerusalem is established shows preparation for homecoming as an active, ongoing task, not passive waiting.

Isaiah 63.summary: A warrior coming from Edom is portrayed with red-stained garments, symbolizing judgment on hostile powers (Isaiah 63:1–6). The remainder recalls God's mercies in the exodus and wilderness, acknowledges rebellion, and pleads for the Lord to return to his people (Isaiah 63:7–19).
Isaiah 63.whereWeAre: Chapter 62 ended with watchmen preparing the way for Zion's restoration. Here a strikingly different figure appears first, a warrior coming from Edom with garments stained red from judgment on hostile powers, before the chapter turns to a communal prayer that recalls God's past mercies in the exodus, confesses rebellion, and pleads for his renewed presence. Chapter 64 continues that same prayer, pressing the plea further and asking God to tear the heavens open.

keyFigures.name: Divine warrior
keyFigures.role: Figure speaking of judgment from Edom.

keyFigures.name: Edom (Bozrah)
keyFigures.role: Geographic setting of the opening vision.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Leader named in the historical recollection.

keyThemes.explanation: A warrior whose garments are stained like someone treading a winepress alone pictures judgment against Edom as thorough and solitary, with no one else to share the work or the blame.
Recalling how God 'bare them, and carried them all the days of old' during the wilderness years grounds the present plea in a specific, remembered history of care.
Asking 'where is he that put his holy Spirit within him?' turns memory of the exodus into a direct, pointed question about where that same presence has gone now.

Isaiah 64.summary: Continuing the communal prayer, the speakers long for God to tear open the heavens and act as in earlier mighty deeds (Isaiah 64:1–4). They confess uncleanness and frailty, address God as potter and father, and lament that Zion and the temple lie in ruins (Isaiah 64:5–12).
Isaiah 64.whereWeAre: Chapter 63 opened a communal prayer recalling God's past mercies. Here that prayer presses further, longing for God to tear open the heavens and act as dramatically as he once did, while the speakers confess their own uncleanness, address God as both potter and father, and lament that Zion and the temple now lie in ruins. Chapter 65 answers this long prayer directly, with God describing exactly how available he has actually been to a rebellious people.

keyFigures.name: Zion and Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Ruined sacred and civic centers in the lament.

keyThemes.explanation: Asking God to tear open the heavens and come down pictures intervention as something dramatic and visible, not a quiet, gradual change.
Calling God 'our father' and themselves clay admits total dependence on him, even while confessing that their own righteousness is 'as filthy rags.'
Naming 'our holy and our beautiful house' as burned turns grief over the temple's destruction into the prayer's most specific, concrete loss.

Isaiah 65.summary: The Lord describes being available to a rebellious people yet confronting idolatry and arrogance (Isaiah 65:1–7). The fate of faithful servants contrasts with that of those rejecting the Lord (Isaiah 65:8–16). A vision of new heavens, new earth, joyful Jerusalem, long life, and peace among animals closes the chapter Isaiah 65:17–25.
Isaiah 65.whereWeAre: Chapter 64 lamented the ruined temple and pleaded for God's intervention. Here God answers directly, describing himself as available all along to a people who simply would not turn to him, even as he distinguishes his faithful servants from those who reject him and promises, beyond all this, new heavens and a new earth where even animals live at peace. Chapter 66 closes the book with one final oracle, combining that same promised joy with a final warning.

keyThemes.explanation: God's statement 'I am sought of them that asked not for me' answers the previous chapter's lament by insisting he was never the one who went missing.
Promising 'new heavens and a new earth' where 'the former shall not be remembered' pictures renewal so complete that even painful memory itself fades.
Long life, lasting homes, and a wolf feeding 'with the lamb' combine human flourishing and peace among animals into one unified picture of restoration.

explainedReferences.explanation: About being found by those who did not seek him.
About reaching out to a disobedient people.

Isaiah 66.summary: God declares that heaven is his throne and no building contains him; he regards the humble who tremble at his word (Isaiah 66:1–4). Zion gives birth suddenly to a people and receives consolation (Isaiah 66:5–14). Judgment falls on idolatry and wickedness, while all nations are gathered to witness glory and worship in a new heavens and earth (Isaiah 66:15–24).
Isaiah 66.whereWeAre: Chapter 65 promised new heavens and a new earth beyond all present ruin. Here the book closes on that same note, combined with a final warning: God declares that no building, however grand, could ever contain him, Zion gives birth to a people suddenly and without labor, and the book ends with nations gathered from everywhere to witness God's glory, even as idolatry and wickedness still face judgment. The next book, Jeremiah, turns from Isaiah's sweeping visions to one prophet's own anguished, personal struggle to warn a nation that will not listen.

keyFigures.name: nations and distant coastlands
keyFigures.role: Peoples gathered to see divine glory.

keyFigures.name: priests and Levites
keyFigures.role: Groups named in the final restoration vision.

keyThemes.explanation: God's preference for 'him that is poor and of a contrite spirit' over any temple, however impressive, redefines true reverence as humility rather than architecture.
Zion giving birth 'before her pain came' pictures restoration arriving with startling, almost impossible suddenness rather than slow recovery.
Nations gathered to 'come, and see my glory' alongside a closing image of unending judgment holds the book's hope and warning together right up to its final verse.

explainedReferences.explanation: Description of heaven as his throne and earth as his footstool.
The warning that the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.
